newsitem.title: GERMANY: German ad industry says tobacco curbs don't work.
newsitem.headline: German ad industry says tobacco curbs don't work.

text.p: Restrictions on tobacco advertising similar to those unveiled last week by U.S. President Bill Clinton would not change German smokers' attitudes, the German Advertising Council (ZAW) said on Monday.
"Calls for a ban on (cigarette) advertising are clearly political charlatanry aimed at confusing the public," ZAW said.

A group of deputies from Chancellor Helmut Kohl's ruling Christian Democrats to the opposition Social Democrats plans to propose tough new anti-smoking legislation in September when the next parliamentary session convenes.
The issue came to the fore when Germany's Federal Court of Labour rejected a complaint by an airline attendant that working on flights where smoking was permitted impaired her health.
But the ad council rejected the notion that there is a link between cigarette advertising and smoking.
"It has been proven beyond doubt that cigarette consumption has not fallen even in countries with complete bans," ZAW said.

In Norway, for example, tobacco advertising has been forbidden since 1975 and prices are twice as high as in Germany, but the proportion of the population that smokes has been steady at 35 percent, it said.
In Britain and Germany, where cigarette advertising is not banned, the smoking population declined in the same period.
Clinton on Friday announced strict rules to control tobacco sales and advertising in a bid to fight teen smoking.
"Populist politicians will have to face the uncomfortable fact that social factors are the main motivation for smokers, particularly among youth," ZAW said.
As Clinton curbs welfare, he is also forced to act against tobacco and alcohol, as a high proportion of the poor in America are under 18, it said.
